alternative: Use std::sync::Arc<T> (or std::rc::Rc<T> when single-threaded): shared ownership with the count in the allocation, one atomic increment per clone, and Weak<T> to break cycles; reserve intrusive counting for foreign objects that already carry a count (GObject, COM, C++ intrusive_ptr), where a small guard type whose Drop calls the foreign release function replaces both the Arc and the count.
idiom_name: none in safe Rust - Arc/Rc keep the count in the allocation; intrusive counts only at FFI edges
implementation_notes: Rust hands out shared ownership through Rc/Arc, which the standard library documents as pointers to a heap allocation whose reference count is increased by clone and whose value is dropped when the last pointer goes - the count belongs to the allocation, not to the value - with Weak available to break cycles that counts can never collect. An intrusive count would live in the value and be reached through shared references, so it needs interior mutability (an atomic field), a guard type with Drop and manual aliasing discipline: exactly the invariant class Rust's ownership rules exist to remove. What replaces the classic structure in safe code: Arc/Rc plus Weak for back-edges; keep the intrusive form only when the counted object is foreign, where Rust owns just the release call.
pitfalls: Arc/Rc cycles are never freed: Weak is mandatory for parent/back pointers, and upgrade() can return None at any time, so every use needs the failure path.

An intrusive counter must be mutated through &self, so it lives in UnsafeCell/atomics and every increment/decrement is an unchecked manual rule - safe-looking code that hides the aliasing risk the type system would otherwise expose.

Wrapping a foreign counted pointer in both Arc and a guard (or copying the raw pointer into two guards) creates two owners of one reference: pick exactly one owner and hand out borrowed references or non-owning guards.
